extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and newspaper journalists (writers of local and feature stories)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for identifying, treating, and writing local-news and small feature items (schools, public institutions, business, human-interest vignettes) so they inform or entertain readers while maintaining journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of miscellaneous local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Local events and institutions that supply material for these stories include schools, public libraries, museums, parks, various departments of city government, real estate, building, manufacturing, business matters, hotels, railroad stations, docks, street cars, and small incidents of daily city life (including animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should look beyond obvious beats to find timely and interesting items in these varied places; many of these form either informative civic items or entertaining sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold purpose (inform vs. entertain)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two classes of local stories: one aims to furnish timely, significant information about public institutions and business activities; the other aims to entertain readers with little glimpses of city life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear which purpose your piece serves and shape content and tone accordingly (informative framing for civic pieces; narrative/entertaining techniques for sketches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utmost accuracy and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost accuracy in presenting information of public affairs and business matters is absolutely essential; the same standard of truthfulness must be maintained in entertaining feature stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fictitious details are no more justifiable in feature stories than in news stories. A newspaper cannot command readers’ confidence if it presents anything in its news columns that is not true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Local stories should furnish timely, significant information; many institutions supported by public money should be of continuing interest to citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select items with immediate public relevance (new openings, administrative changes, enrollment figures, institutional problems) and give prominence to time-sensitive facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize public significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive journalism should stimulate the interest of every citizen in municipal affairs and public institutions by putting significant information prominently before the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with facts that show why the story matters to the community; highlight consequences, budgets, scope, and public impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attractive form and stylistic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: To interest the average reader in municipal activities it is necessary to make the stories attractive in form and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, readable prose; make the lead engaging; adapt style to audience—civic pieces more direct, entertaining sketches more literary—but never at the expense of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use striking facts, figures, and unusual statements at the opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking facts and figures or unusual statements, featured at the beginning, catch the reader’s eye and lead him to read the story as long as its subject matter and style interest him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with comparisons, surprising statistics, or an arresting statement (the text cites the example of beginning with comparisons to armies and budgets to show scale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective use of statistics and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective use of statistics and comparisons helps demonstrate significance and attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present numbers and comparisons clearly and contextually so readers grasp scale and importance; avoid misleading or decontextualized figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative and descriptive devices for entertaining features
rubrics_metrics.description: For entertaining feature stories, narrative and descriptive beginnings, conversation, suspense, humor, and other short-story devices are well adapted to these news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since entertaining features may lack news urgency, hold the reader by telling the story well—use scene-setting, dialogue, suspense, and humor where appropriate while preserving factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and develop human-interest vignettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Little incidents in the daily life of every city that have no significance as news can be written up as entertaining stories; hotels, stations, docks, and street cars often provide scenes for comedies and tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters with keen insight into human life and ability to portray it can turn small events and characters into readable sketches; include sensory detail and precise observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match technique to the story’s news interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Because entertaining feature stories often lack news interest, the writer must rely on storytelling methods to attract attention; conversely, informative municipal pieces depend on clear presentation of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early whether the value of the piece lies in its information or in its narrative, and apply appropriate techniques (facts-first leads vs. scene-setting leads) while maintaining the same factual standards.
